analysis.one_liner: Rewrites the rulemaking process so federal agencies must generally adopt the cheapest regulation that meets statutory goals.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with bipartisan cosponsorship in September 2011 but never received a committee markup or floor vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite how federal agencies write major rules. Agencies would have to prove a rule's benefits justify its costs, consider cheaper alternatives, and by default adopt the least expensive option that meets the law's goals. Rules expected to cost the economy $1 billion or more a year would require formal, trial-style hearings where regulated parties can cross-examine agency witnesses, and companies would get expanded ability to challenge rules in court, including immediate review of emergency interim rules. Supporters framed this as reducing red tape and improving the quality of regulation; the practical effect would be to make major protections—on workplace safety, pollution, food safety, and finance—slower, costlier to defend, and easier to block.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies and industries regulated by federal rules—manufacturers, energy and chemical firms, financial companies and their trade associations—would gain procedural tools to delay, weaken, or defeat rules they consider expensive. Formal hearings with cross-examination, a default to the cheapest rule, and broader court access give regulated parties more opportunities to stall rules for years. Law firms and compliance consultants would also gain from the added litigation and paperwork.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries and their trade associations

how_it_helps.text: Agencies would be required to adopt the least costly rule that meets the relevant statutory objectives unless they justify a costlier choice in terms of public health, safety, or welfare.

Major and high-impact rules would require advance notice of proposed rulemaking with extended comment periods, formal cost-benefit determinations, and—for rules costing $1 billion or more a year—a trial-style hearing with cross-examination of the agency's factual case.

The bill expands judicial review, allowing immediate court challenges to interim rules issued without full procedures and directing courts to review agency rules under a substantial evidence standard without deferring to agency economic or risk determinations that fail to conform to White House guidelines.
Every major rule would have to be reviewed at least every ten years to determine whether it is still needed and whether it can be modified or rescinded to reduce costs.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost through delayed or weaker federal protections: rules on workplace safety, clean air and water, product safety, and financial misconduct would take longer to issue, face more avenues for legal challenge, and be pushed toward the cheapest option rather than the most protective one that the law allows. Agency budgets and timelines would also bear the burden of the added hearings and analyses, and court dockets would absorb a wave of new challenges.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on federal health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: A good-faith objection: federal rulemaking is genuinely slow, opaque, and expensive, and some rules impose costs far out of proportion to their benefits. Requiring agencies to prove benefits justify costs, consider alternatives, and review old rules every decade could improve the quality of regulation and make the process more transparent.

Making the least costly rule the legal default flips the traditional cost-benefit balance: an agency choosing a more protective rule would have to defend that choice in formal hearings and court, which would discourage agencies from issuing strong protections at all.

Trial-style hearings with cross-examination for billion-dollar rules would draw out rulemaking for years, and immediate judicial review of interim rules could leave emergency protections—such as a rapid response to a health hazard—vulnerable to being tied up or voided in court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's transparency provisions—public dockets, cost-benefit statements, and ten-year reviews—have real value on their own. But its central mechanics are tilted toward the regulated: a cheapest-rule default, formal hearings on the agency's factual case, and broad new avenues to sue. That combination would make it substantially harder for agencies to issue strong health, safety, environmental, and financial rules, and the delay itself is often a win for the regulated party even if the rule eventually survives. The design serves the interests of regulated firms far more than it improves outcomes for the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in September 2011, and the committee never took it up before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Rob Portman introduced the bill on September 22, 2011, joined by Sens. Mark Pryor and Susan Collins.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, where it remained.
The bill attracted 8 cosponsors, 3 Democrats and 5 Republicans, but received no further committee or floor action.
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, without the bill ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies and the people who rely on their rules came out ahead: the existing rulemaking process, with its more flexible cost-benefit balancing, remained intact because the bill never advanced. Industries seeking the bill's procedural barriers gained nothing from its death, though they also lost nothing they already had.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on existing federal rules

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sen. Mark Pryor of Arkansas, who helped introduce it.

for.what_they_did: Championed regulatory accountability legislation in this era as a top legislative priority for its business members.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee consideration of the bill, leaving it without a markup or vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship—8 cosponsors split 3 Democrats and 5 Republicans—but neither party's leadership brought it to a committee markup or a floor vote.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturing, energy, chemical, and financial firms)
industries.note: The bill would give regulated companies formal hearings, a cheapest-rule default, and expanded court access—tools for delaying, weakening, or blocking health, safety, environmental, and financial rules. The delay and the shift toward lower-cost rules transfer protection costs from firms onto the public.

industries.industry: Law firms and regulatory compliance consultants
industries.note: Expanded litigation rights and mandatory formal hearings would create new billable work in challenges to federal rules, and companies would need more consultants to satisfy the detailed analytic requirements. The gains come from a slower, more adversarial process, not from better public outcomes.

industries.industry: Public health, safety, and environmental enforcement agencies
industries.note: Agencies would face mandatory hearings, stricter evidentiary standards, expanded court review, and a legal default to the cheapest rule, all of which would slow or deter protective rulemaking. Their loss in enforcement capacity is the public's loss as well.
